analysis.one_liner: Gives candidates six dollars of public matching funds for every small donation, and caps large contributions.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee hearing or a vote; it had no cosponsors and died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rebuild the public financing system for presidential elections and create one for congressional elections. Candidates who qualify would get six dollars of public money for every dollar raised in small contributions, but only if they agreed to accept no contribution over $1,000 from any person and no bundled money from registered lobbyists. It would also raise the tax-form checkoff that funds the system and require more disclosure of who bundles contributions for presidential campaigns.
analysis.who_benefits: Candidates who run on small donations from many people instead of a few large checks, and voters who want elections funded by the public rather than by big donors and bundlers.

how_it_helps.text: Congressional candidates who collect enough small contributions (400 donors and $40,000 for a House candidate, scaled for Senate candidates) would get 600% matching public funds, up to $2 million for a House race and $10 million for a Senate race.

To qualify, candidates must cap individual contributions at $1,000 per person per election and refuse bundled contributions forwarded by registered lobbyists, reducing the leverage of large donors and lobbying interests over campaigns.
Presidential primary and general candidates would get the same 600% match on small contributions, up to $300 million, while current spending-limit rules are replaced with these contribution limits.

The checkoff on income tax forms that funds presidential public financing would rise from $3 to $20 per taxpayer and be indexed to inflation, and taxpayers could add a voluntary donation; the bill also bars tax software from automatically answering the checkoff question for people.

Presidential campaigns would have to disclose the name, address, and employer of anyone bundling more than $50,000 in contributions, extending lobbyist bundling disclosure rules to all presidential campaign bundlers.

analysis.who_pays: The program is funded through the existing voluntary tax checkoff (raised to $20) and optional taxpayer donations, plus Treasury advances for the first cycle; the real cost falls on campaigns financed by large donors and bundlers, who would lose access to candidates who join the system.

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals spending limits for participating candidates while offering a 6-to-1 match up to $300 million for presidential candidates and $10 million for Senate candidates, so public outlays could be very large and are funded partly through repayable Treasury advances in the first cycle.

The checkoff amount rises from $3 to $20 of tax liability per taxpayer, and only taxpayers who actively designate pay into it; if participation stays low, general Treasury advances and supplemental appropriations would cover the gap.

Participation is voluntary, so candidates who decline public funds could still raise unlimited large contributions subject to existing limits, and the bill applies no new limits to outside spending by groups that make independent expenditures beyond a $5,000 annual cap on donations to such committees.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: public matching money would make small donors the dominant funding source for participating campaigns, at a fiscal cost financed through a voluntary checkoff rather than a tax increase. The main design weakness is that the bill pairs generous matching funds with repealed spending limits, which invites high public spending, and it leaves outside independent spending largely untouched. But its headline effect is to shift campaign money from large donors toward small contributors.

outcome.mechanism: Udall introduced it and it was sent to the Senate Rules and Administration Committee, which never held a hearing or vote, and the bill expired when the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Sen. Tom Udall introduced the bill on October 5, 2017.
The same day it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Rules and Administration, its only committee referral.
No further action was ever taken: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and the bill had zero cosponsors.
The bill expired on January 3, 2019, when the 115th Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Candidates and parties that rely on large contributions and lobbyist bundling kept the fundraising system unchanged, and no public money was spent on campaign financing.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so how members would have split is unknown from the record; all that is documented is a single Democratic sponsor, zero cosponsors from either party, and no action in the Republican-majority Senate.

industries.note: The bill would cap contributions to participating candidates at $1,000 per person and bar accepting bundled contributions from registered lobbyists, shrinking the access that six- and seven-figure givers currently buy. Bundlers' influence would drop further since presidential campaigns must disclose anyone bundling over $50,000.

Lobbyists can currently bundle large sums for candidates; the bill would ban participating candidates from accepting their bundled money and require public disclosure of bundling activity at lower thresholds.

The bill would repeal the special high-limit accounts that let big donors give up to three times the normal limit to national parties, but would also raise the coordinated-expenditure limit for presidential races to $100 million and allow unlimited coordinated spending on behalf of participating candidates when funded by small-dollar contributions.

Funding comes from a voluntary tax-form checkoff raised from $3 to $20 and optional donations, with Treasury advances covering the first cycle; it is not a new tax, but public money would flow to campaigns, which some taxpayers would support and others would not.
